newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt opens natural gas grid to its private sector.
newsitem.headline: Egypt opens natural gas grid to its private sector.

text.p: Egypt has decided for the first time to allow its private sector to finance and build natural gas grids and market the gas, an official statement said.

Oil Minister Hamdi el-Banbi's decision puts another crack in Egypt's monolithic state-dominated economy, where the private sector has been slowly gaining a foothold since the state began implementing reforms in earnest in early 1996.

The statement, obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, said Banbi "announced approval of the participation of the private sector for the first time in financing and construction of natural gas grids and marketing of the gas."
It is also the latest sign that the Egyptian private sector is slowly increasing its role in the oil and gas industry.

"It's a very positive sign that they are letting the private sector have a greater role in such an important industry," an international economist said. "It is consistent with what the government has said about the oil and natural gas industries."
Last month, private firm Ghareb Oil Fields started producing oil from its Burg al-Arab field, which was the country's first oil discovery by a private Egyptian firm.
The firm's chairman Saleh Mahmoud Awadallah told Reuters at the time the firm would produce some 70,000 bpd after five years, and he saw great natural gas potential in the concession.
The private sector also has a minority stake in a gas firm set up in March by three majority state-owned companies.

The Egyptian Company for Natural Gases (GASCO) was set up by the state Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC), Petrojet and Egypt Gas with an issued capital of 221 million pounds ($65 million) to build, operate and own gas pipelines, distribution facilities and processing plants. Officials said they would increase the GASCO's capital through a public offer.
Mohammad Ibrahim Taweela, GASCO vice chairman and managing director, told Reuters on Wednesday that he saw a role for GASCO in the new decision.

"We'll apply for some areas and make some feasibility studies and surveys and provide EGPC with proposals in addition to our current activity," he said. "Our main activity is gas processing, but we will also be involved in implementing the new concept of gas distribution."
Egypt has reduced its role in state holding companies, but has moved more slowly in so-called strategic sectors of milling, and some aspects of the oil sector, power and banks.
"This is a great stride on Egypt's part. They've got sizeable national gas resources in Egypt and this is one way of capitalising on that," said Jim House, operations manager of Apache oil company.
Natural gas output was 1.173 billion cubic feet a day in June.
